title: McGuffey's Fourth Eclectic Reader
sourceTitle: McGuffey's Fourth Eclectic Reader, Revised Edition
author: William Holmes McGuffey
licenseEvidence: Project Gutenberg eBook #14880: 'Public domain in the USA.' Revised edition first copyrighted 1879 (Van Antwerp, Bragg & Co.); renewals 1896 (American Book Company) and 1907 and 1920 (H. H. Vail), all before 1930.
description: The classic Fourth Reader: 90 stories, poems, and short essays, from fairy tales and animal anecdotes to Longfellow, Hawthorne, Defoe, and Louisa May Alcott. Each day your child learns the lesson's own vocabulary, reads aloud, and narrates or memorizes a few lines, with a couple of questions to talk over. The full text is free online.
includes: 92 lessons in 9 units: two getting-started lessons plus all 90 Fourth Reader selections
Link to the free full text for every lesson
Vocabulary from each lesson's own definitions, a read-aloud, and a narration or memory-work step every day
Authors named and parent notes on sad, dated, or sensitive content

units.title: Unit 1: Getting Started and Lessons I–X

lessons.title: Getting Started: Punctuation Marks
steps: Read through the eighteen punctuation marks together, saying what each one tells the reader
Find a comma, a semicolon, a question mark, and quotation marks in today's newspaper or a favorite book
Copywork: write one sentence that uses quotation marks and an apostrophe
questions: What do quotation marks show?
What does an apostrophe show?
What is a caret (^) used for?
answers: The words of another person
That a letter or letters are left out
To show, in writing, where something was left out
lessons.notes: The book's introductory pages. Come back to this list whenever a lesson asks about a mark.

lessons.title: Getting Started: Articulation, Accent, and Inflection
steps: Say the vowel and consonant sounds in the tables aloud, slowly and clearly
Practice a few rows of the 'Errors to be Corrected' (for example, saying 'and,' not 'an'; 'morning,' not 'mornin')
Read the inflection examples, letting your voice rise on questions like “Has he come?” and fall on “They are here.”
questions: What is inflection?
Does the voice usually rise or fall at the end of a question like “Has he come?”
answers: An upward or downward slide of the voice
It rises
lessons.notes: Use a few minutes of these drills before lessons during the year rather than doing them all at once.

lessons.title: Lesson I: Perseverance
steps: New words: entangled (twisted in), disengaged (set free), dignity (majestic manner), disappointments, perseverance (keeping on with what you began), motto
Read the lesson aloud together, taking turns by paragraph
Narrate: tell every way the kite failed before it finally flew
questions: Why did John want to quit?
What did John say he had learned from the morning?
What motto did the aunt give the children?
answers: The kite kept falling and he was tired of being bothered with it
How to fly his kite properly
Try again
lessons.notes: By Charlotte Elizabeth.

lessons.title: Lesson II: Try, Try Again
steps: New words: courage, conquer (win), prevail (overcome), disgrace (shame), patience
Read the poem aloud, letting your child say the repeated line each time
Memorize: the first stanza (“'T is a lesson you should heed…”)
questions: What does the apostrophe in “'T is” stand for?
According to the poem, is it a disgrace to lose a race if you tried?
answers: The missing letter i in “It is”
No; if we strive, losing is no disgrace
lessons.notes: Poem by T. H. Palmer. A favorite for memorizing.

lessons.title: Lesson III: Why the Sea Is Salt (Part 1)
steps: New words: trifling (of small value), hand mill, attracted, perplexed (puzzled), fragrance
Read the fairy tale aloud, you and your child alternating paragraphs
Narrate: how did the poor brother get the magic mill?
questions: What did the rich brother give the poor brother?
What did the old man tell him to ask the dwarfs for instead of money?
What was the first thing the mill ground out at home?
answers: A ham
The old hand mill behind the door
Lighted candles, a fire, and a boiling porridge pot
lessons.notes: A Norse fairy tale retold by Mary Howitt.

lessons.title: Lesson IV: Why the Sea Is Salt (Part 2)
steps: New words: devoutly (reverently), reflecting, landmark, extraordinary, whirlpool, peasants
Read the conclusion aloud; let your child read the merchant's commands with expression
Narrate: what happened to the mill in the end, and why?
Find Denmark and Norway on a map
questions: Why would the brother not lend the mill to the rich man?
How did the merchant get the mill?
Why, says the tale, is the sea salt?
answers: The old man told him never to sell or lend it
He bribed a servant and stole it
The stolen mill sank and still grinds salt at the bottom of the sea
lessons.notes: Talk about how this is a 'why' tale people once told for fun, and what the real reason is (salts washed from rocks by rivers).

lessons.title: Lesson V: Popping Corn
steps: Read the poem aloud twice, the second time with your child joining in the pops
Copywork: “Pop! pop! and the kernels, one by one,”
Narrate: describe the scene by the kitchen fire
questions: What was the weather like that night?
What did the little sister call the heap of popped corn?
answers: Windy and rainy
A flock of milk-white sheep
lessons.notes: Short poem; good day to pop some corn together.

lessons.title: Lesson VI: Smiles
steps: New words: dismal (gloomy), wishfully, rickety (worn out), dingy (dark), dreary, contrive (to plan)
Read the story aloud, taking the parts of Jennie, George, and Mrs. West
Narrate: how did George make Jennie's day brighter?
questions: Why did Jennie have to sit at the window all day?
Why had Jennie's family moved to the city?
What did George's mother say we can always give?
answers: She was lame
Her father died, her mother was ill, and the money ran out
Smiles, with a kind word

lessons.title: Lesson VII: Lazy Ned
steps: New words: royal (excellent), coast (to slide), indolent (lazy), bugbear (something frightening), dunce
Read the poem aloud with feeling
Copywork: “To seek the prize that labor gains,”
questions: What did Ned love to do?
What part did he hate?
answers: Coast down the hill on his sled
Climbing back up the hill

lessons.title: Lesson VIII: The Monkey
steps: New words: cunning (sly), toilet table (dressing table), missiles, exhibitions, gravity (seriousness)
Your child reads aloud while you follow along
Narrate: tell the story of the monkey and the doll, or the monkey and the dog
questions: What was the monkey doing at the toilet table?
What happened to Maria's doll?
Do wild monkeys use sticks as weapons, according to the lesson?
answers: Brushing his teeth while looking in the mirror
The monkey washed its face so hard the paint came off
No; they can only be taught to
lessons.notes: The dog-and-monkey fight was staged for sport by organ grinders; a good place to talk about kindness to animals.

lessons.title: Lesson IX: Meddlesome Matty
steps: New words: qualities, meddling (interfering), forthwith (at once), amiss (wrong), woeful, tingling
Read the poem aloud, one stanza each
Narrate: what happened when Matilda opened the box?
questions: What was Matilda's one bad fault?
What two things of grandmamma's did she meddle with?
What did she promise afterward?
answers: Meddling with things
Her spectacles and her snuffbox
Never to meddle again
lessons.notes: Poem by Ann Taylor (not named in the book). Snuff was powdered tobacco sniffed through the nose.

lessons.title: Lesson X: The Good Son
steps: New words: jeweler, elder, ephod (part of a high priest's dress), humor (temper), close (come to an agreement)
Read the story aloud together
Narrate: why did the jeweler wait, and what price did he finally accept?
questions: Why couldn't the jeweler show the diamonds right away?
Which price did he accept in the end?
Which commandment did the elders quote?
answers: His father was asleep with the key, and he would not wake him
The first price they had offered
Honor thy father and thy mother
lessons.notes: Based on a story from the Jewish Talmud.

lessons.title: Lesson XI: To-morrow
steps: New words: household, elf, vex (worry), pondered (thought hard), awhile
Read the poem aloud, your child reading Eddie's questions and you the mother's answers
Narrate: why could Eddie never catch to-morrow?
questions: What question kept troubling Eddie?
What did his mother tell him to do instead of waiting for to-morrow?
answers: When will to-morrow come?
Enjoy to-day
lessons.notes: Poem by Mrs. M. B. Johnson.

lessons.title: Lesson XII: Where There Is a Will There Is a Way
steps: New words: management, furnish (supply), furiously, service (labor), premises (grounds around a house)
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Narrate: how did Henry get his grammar book?
questions: What book did Henry need?
How did he earn the money for it?
What saying did he remember when he saw the snow?
answers: A grammar
By shoveling paths through the snow for neighbors
It is an ill wind that blows nobody good

lessons.title: Lesson XIII: Piccola
steps: New words: dawned, befall (happen), shivering, tiny, rapture (great joy)
Read the poem aloud with expression
Narrate: what did Piccola find in her shoe, and how did she feel?
questions: Why were Piccola's parents sad on Christmas morning?
What was in Piccola's shoe?
In what country did Piccola live?
answers: They were too poor to give her a gift
A little shivering sparrow
France
lessons.notes: Poem by Celia Thaxter. 'Drive the wolf from the door' means to keep from starving.

lessons.title: Lesson XIV: True Manliness (Part 1)
steps: New words: languidly (feebly), amply (fully), opinion, absolutely, resent, consciousness
Read the story aloud, taking turns by paragraph
Narrate: how did Fred help at home, and how did the boys treat him?
questions: Why did Fred wash the dishes and do the housework?
Who spied on Fred through the kitchen window?
How did the teacher stop the teasing?
answers: His mother was ill and needed rest
Tom Barton
He told the boys Fred must not be teased
lessons.notes: By Mrs. M. O. Johnson. The boys' teasing assumes housework is only for girls; a good point to discuss.

lessons.title: Lesson XV: True Manliness (Part 2)
steps: Read the conclusion aloud; your child reads the fire scene with feeling
Narrate: tell how Katy was saved
Talk about it: what does 'true manliness' mean at the end of the story?
questions: Whose house was on fire?
How did Fred reach Katy?
What did Tom Barton learn?
answers: Mr. Barton's (Tom's family's)
He climbed a ladder and broke in through the window
True manliness goes with gentleness, kindness, and self-denial

lessons.title: Lesson XVI: The Brown Thrush
steps: Read the poem aloud; let your child be the thrush
Memorize: the first stanza (“There's a merry brown thrush sitting up in a tree…”)
Look up a picture of a brown thrasher or thrush and listen to its song if you can
questions: How many eggs were in the thrush's nest?
In what kind of tree was the nest?
What does the thrush ask children not to do?
answers: Five
A juniper tree
Meddle with or touch the nest
lessons.notes: Poem by Lucy Larcom.

lessons.title: Lesson XVII: A Ship in a Storm
steps: New words: echoed, gale, heaves, billows (waves), desperate, gratitude, luxuries
Read the lesson aloud together
Narrate: tell how the man overboard was rescued
Talk about lighthouses, fog horns, and life-saving stations
questions: What do sailors do when they see a storm coming?
How did they get the boat back onto the rolling ship?
How do lighthouses warn ships when fog hides the light?
answers: Take in the sails
They hoisted it up by a rope and it fell onto the deck
With fog bells or fog horns
lessons.notes: Life-saving stations were the forerunner of today's Coast Guard.

lessons.title: Lesson XVIII: The Sailor's Consolation
steps: New words: hurricane, quid (piece of chewing tobacco), foolhardy, notion, spouses, chimney pots
Read the poem aloud in a hearty sailor's voice
Narrate: why does Barney feel sorry for people on land? Is he right?
questions: What were the two sailors' names?
What dangers does Barney think landsmen face?
Is the poem serious or joking?
answers: Barney Buntline and Billy Bowling
Falling roofs and chimney pots, overturned carriages, thieves, and fires
Joking; the sailors are in far greater danger
lessons.notes: Poem by Charles Dibdin, an 18th-century writer of sea songs. Barney chews tobacco.

lessons.title: Lesson XIX: Two Ways of Telling a Story
steps: New words: populous, excursion (pleasure trip), incidents, warrant, capsized (upset), venerable (worthy of respect)
Read the lesson aloud; your child reads the boy's story and you read the teacher's
Narrate: tell the same sleigh ride first as the boys saw it, then as the old man felt it
questions: What did the boys do to the slow wagon?
Who was the old man in the wagon?
Were the boys mostly cruel or thoughtless?
answers: Pelted it with snowballs, cheered, and whipped the horse
The teacher's father, an old minister
Mostly thoughtless, though it was still unkind
lessons.notes: By Henry K. Oliver.

lessons.title: Lesson XX: Freaks of the Frost
steps: New words: blustering, bustle, crest (top), quivering, margin (edge), bevies (flocks), sheen
Read the poem aloud slowly, enjoying the pictures
Narrate: list all the places the Frost visited and what he did there
On a frosty morning, look for frost pictures on a window
questions: What did the Frost spread over the lake?
What pictures did he draw on the windows?
What mischief did he do in the cupboard?
answers: A coat of mail (ice)
Flowers, trees, birds, bees, and cities with towers
Bit the fruit, burst the pitcher, and cracked the glass of water
lessons.notes: Poem by Hannah Flagg Gould. A 'coat of mail' is armor; the 'spears' are icicles.

lessons.title: Lesson XXI: Waste Not, Want Not
steps: New words: examine, signifies (matters), marksman, prudently (with caution), ceased
Read it as a play: one person is Ben, one John, one Mr. Jones and Master Sharp
Narrate: how did a saved piece of string win the archery prize?
questions: How did Ben and John open their parcels differently?
What did Ben use the whipcord for the first time?
Why couldn't John borrow Ben's bow at the match?
answers: Ben untied the knot; John cut the string
As a string for his new top
The rules said no borrowing or lending
lessons.notes: Adapted from Maria Edgeworth's story of the same name.

lessons.title: Lesson XXII: Jeannette and Jo
steps: Read the poem aloud; your child takes Jo's grumbling lines
Copywork: “The hopeful are the gladdest;”
Narrate: how did the two girls act differently in the shower?
questions: Which girl was always moping?
What did Jo cry when the rain came?
What did Jeannette do instead?
answers: Jo
“It always is a-raining!”
Waited hopefully until the sun came out
lessons.notes: Poem by Mary Mapes Dodge, author of Hans Brinker.

lessons.title: Lesson XXIII: The Lion
steps: New words: majestic, prowls, unawares (unexpectedly), rumble, menagerie (collection of wild animals), heroic
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Narrate: tell the story of Danco and his keeper William
questions: Why is the lion called the king of beasts?
When does the lion usually hunt?
What did Danco do when the carpenter cried out?
answers: For his great strength and majestic mane
At night
Put his paw on his sleeping keeper as if to guard him
lessons.notes: Wild lions today live mainly in Africa, with a small group in India; the lion-keeper story is an old anecdote, not safe behavior.

lessons.title: Lesson XXIV: Strawberries
steps: New words: thrive, nestled, mold (soft earth), runner, mellow (ripen), dial, pelf (money)
Read the poem aloud; your child reads the berries' part
Narrate: what did the berries say about their year from winter to June?
questions: How old was Pearl Honeydew?
What covered the berries in winter?
In what month do the berries ripen?
answers: Six
Snow
June
lessons.notes: Poem by J. T. Trowbridge. The berries talking is a kind of make-believe called personification.

lessons.title: Lesson XXV: Harry's Riches
steps: New words: disconsolate (full of grief), reproachfully, chloroform, defiantly, experiments, exultingly, treasures
Read the story aloud, your child taking Harry's part and you Uncle Ben's
Narrate: how did Uncle Ben show Harry that he was rich?
questions: Why did Harry think he was poor?
What were the first two things Uncle Ben offered to buy?
What did Harry decide at the end?
answers: His friend Johnny had money and many toys
His eyes and his hearing
That God makes everybody rich
lessons.notes: Uncle Ben's offers are only a pretend game to make a point; reassure a sensitive child.

lessons.title: Lesson XXVI: In Time's Swing
steps: New words: twittering, glimpse (quick look), blur, rime (white frost)
Read the poem aloud, one stanza per season
Narrate: name the flowers and birds the swing passes, from spring to December
Copywork: “Swing me low, and swing me high,”
questions: Who is pushing the swing?
How many pushes does the child ask for, and what do they stand for?
Where does the swing end up?
answers: Father Time
Twelve, one for each month
From the Old Year into the New
lessons.notes: Poem by Lucy Larcom.

lessons.title: Lesson XXVII: Harry and His Dog
steps: New words: inverted (upside down), porringer, plight, pensioner, pilferers, vigilant (watchful), forfeited (lost)
Read the story aloud together
Narrate: how did Frisk repay Harry's kindness, even after a bad day?
questions: How did Frisk first come to Milton?
How did Frisk earn his place in the house?
What did Frisk bring Harry in bed?
answers: As a wet, starving stray
By barking away thieves from the pear tree
A big pear
lessons.notes: By Mary Russell Mitford.

lessons.title: Lesson XXVIII: The Voice of the Grass
steps: Read the poem aloud softly; your child joins on “creeping, creeping, everywhere”
Copywork: “Here I come, creeping, creeping, everywhere;”
Narrate: list the places the grass says it grows
questions: Who is speaking in this poem?
Which animal is glad to see the grass?
To whom does the grass raise its song of praise?
answers: The grass
The cow
God, who commands it to beautify the land
lessons.notes: Poem by Sarah Roberts. One stanza gently mentions graves.

lessons.title: Lesson XXIX: The Eagle
steps: New words: supremacy, talons, carcass, species, emblem, relinquish (give up)
Your child reads aloud while you look up pictures of a golden eagle and a bald eagle
Narrate: tell what you learned about the three kinds of eagle
questions: Which eagle is the emblem of the United States?
What does the bald eagle mainly eat?
How does the bald eagle often steal its food?
answers: The bald eagle
Fish
By forcing the fish hawk (osprey) to drop its catch
lessons.notes: Old natural history: the claims that eagles carry off children and that one lived 104 years are legends, not fact.

lessons.title: Lesson XXX: The Old Eagle Tree
steps: New words: gigantic, sublime (grand), dispersed (scattered), unavailing (useless), clamorous (loud), exhausted
Read the story aloud, taking turns
Narrate: what did the eagle do after her fish was stolen?
questions: What kind of tree held the eagle's nest?
How did the workmen get the eagle's fish?
What lesson did Joseph take from the eagle?
answers: A tall tulip tree
They yelled, hooted, and threw stones until she dropped it
Never give up when discouraged
lessons.notes: By Dr. John Todd.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXI: Alpine Song
steps: New words: alpenstock (iron-pointed walking staff), knapsack, chalet (mountain hut), list (listen to)
Read the poem aloud with a light, marching rhythm
Memorize: the refrain “Free in heart—happy and free— / This is the summer life for me.”
Find the Alps on a map
questions: Where does the hiker sleep?
What sound does he hear in the upland meadows?
answers: In a chalet (mountain hut)
The bells of wandering herds
lessons.notes: Poem by William Wetmore Story.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXII: Circumstances Alter Cases
steps: New words: whimsical, curried (brushed), bungler (clumsy worker), disposed (willing), crammed
Read it as a play: one of you is Derby, the other Scrapewell (and Tim)
Narrate: why did Scrapewell suddenly lend the mare?
questions: What did Derby want to borrow?
Name two excuses Scrapewell gave.
What changed Scrapewell's mind?
answers: Scrapewell's gray mare
Any two: going to the mill, she won't eat hay, it's slippery, broken saddle, no shoes, a sore back
Hearing he could share in a fifty-dollar timber deal
lessons.notes: A comic dialogue; talk about why the title fits. Fifty dollars was a large sum then.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIII: The Noblest Revenge
steps: New words: revenge, repent, countenance (face), induced (caused), contempt (scorn), inflict, agony
Read the story aloud; your child takes Philip's part, you take Stephen's
Narrate: what revenge did Philip finally take on young Robinson?
questions: How did Philip's cane get broken?
What happened when Robinson tried to get revenge on a bee?
What did Philip call 'the noblest vengeance'?
answers: It accidentally upset Robinson's pitcher, and Robinson twisted it in anger
He poked the hive and the whole swarm stung him
Returning good for evil

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIV: Evening Hymn
steps: Read the hymn aloud slowly and quietly, as at the end of a day
Memorize: the first stanza (“Come to the sunset tree…”)
Narrate: what rest does the poem promise at the end?
questions: Whose work is done in the first stanza?
What will there be no more of in the world beyond, according to the last stanza?
answers: The woodman's and the reaper's
Tempests, scorching heat, snow, and weary wandering feet
lessons.notes: Poem by Felicia Hemans (not named in the book). A good bedtime reading.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXV: How Margery Wondered
steps: New words: trudging, hues (colors), calyx (outer cup of a flower), horizon, warble, sheaths
Read the story aloud; pause at each of Margery's questions
Narrate: name the things Margery wondered about
Go outside and find one thing to wonder about, as Margery did
questions: What bird did Margery see for the first time?
What did the sun look like to her?
What did Margery's mother say when Margery wanted to live on the doorstep?
answers: A bluebird
A great golden flower without a stem
“Queer child! I wonder what kind of a woman she will be!”
lessons.notes: By Lucy Larcom.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVI: The Child's World
steps: Read the poem aloud with wonder in your voice
Memorize: the first stanza (“Great, wide, beautiful, wonderful world…”)
Narrate: what does the whisper inside the child say at the end?
questions: What does the wind do in the second stanza?
How is the child greater than the Earth?
answers: Shakes the tree, walks on the water, whirls the mills, and talks on the hilltops
The child can love and think, and the Earth cannot
lessons.notes: Poem by William Brighty Rands (not named in the book).

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVII: Susie's Composition
steps: New words: composition, rumpled, themes (topics), request, occupation, bouquets
Read the story aloud together
Write it: sit by a window for ten minutes and write about what you see, as Susie did
questions: What three topics had Susie tried to write about?
What did her mother tell her to do instead?
Why was it easy to write the second time?
answers: Time, Temperance, and Industry
Look out the window and write about what she saw
She had something interesting that she knew about to write about

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVIII: The Summer Shower
steps: New words: aslant (slanting), highway, retreat (shelter), crouches, taunting, urchin (child)
Read the poem aloud, letting the rhythm gallop like the rain
Copywork: “That the beautiful bow bendeth over them all.”
Narrate: what does each creature do while it rains?
questions: What does the poet compare the slanting rain to?
Which birds keep flying in the storm?
What appears over everyone at the end?
answers: A long line of shining spears (also galloping cavalry)
The swallows
A rainbow
lessons.notes: Poem by Thomas Buchanan Read.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIX: Consequences of Idleness
steps: New words: consequence, academy, preceptor (teacher), alacrity (cheerful readiness), ludicrous, dissipated (given to bad habits)
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Narrate: tell what happened to George Jones at the academy and then at college
questions: Why did the other boys choose George last for games?
Why was college so much harder for George than the academy?
What happened to George in the end?
answers: He was moping and dull even at play
He had fallen too far behind to keep up, and many students saw him fail
He was sent away from college and became a poor, friendless wanderer
lessons.notes: Paired with the next lesson. Its picture of school and 'reciting' is old-fashioned; the point is the habit of steady work.

lessons.title: Lesson XL: Advantages of Industry
steps: New words: conscience, committed (fixed in mind), tranquil (calm), conferred (given), commencement, universally, invariably (always)
Read the lesson aloud, taking turns by paragraph
Narrate: compare Charles Bullard's school days with George Jones's from the last lesson
Copywork: “With books, or work, or healthful play, / Let your first years be passed;”
questions: Did Charles skip play to study?
What honor did Charles receive at college?
According to the lesson, what does hard study do for play?
answers: Only rarely, when lessons were very hard; usually he played and was one of the best players
He was chosen to give the society's yearly public address
It gives you a relish for play (and play gives a relish for study)
lessons.notes: The closing paragraph links diligence with being right with God; families can discuss it in their own way.

lessons.title: Lesson XLI: The Fountain
steps: New words: blithesome (gay), cheery, aweary (tired), aspiring, element, constant
Read the short lines aloud quickly, like leaping water
Memorize: the last stanza (“Glorious fountain! / Let my heart be…”)
questions: At what times of day is the fountain happy?
What does the poet ask his heart to be like?
answers: All the time: sunshine, moonlight, starlight, midnight, and day
Fresh, changeful, constant, and upward like the fountain
lessons.notes: Poem by James Russell Lowell.

lessons.title: Lesson XLII: Coffee
steps: New words: afforded (produced), offspring, pliable (easily bent), translucent, pruning, aromatic
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Narrate: tell how coffee traveled from Africa and Arabia to the rest of the world
Find Arabia, Java, Holland, and South America on a map
questions: Where is the coffee tree native?
What does the coffee fruit look like when ripe?
Why are coffee plants pruned short?
answers: Eastern Africa
Like a dark red cherry
So the gatherers can reach the fruit easily
lessons.notes: Some trade and history details are dated; Brazil, Vietnam, and Colombia are major growers today.

lessons.title: Lesson XLIII: The Winter King
steps: New words: muttering, unconscious (not aware), cluster, flitting, vesture (clothing), monitor, oracle
Read it aloud; you ask the questions and your child answers as the bird with “Pee, dee, dee!”
Narrate: how does the little bird answer each worry?
questions: What was the bird eating?
How does the bird keep its bare feet warm?
Why is it called the Winter King?
answers: Gum from the old peach tree
It draws them up into its feathers
Because it is merry and free in all weather
lessons.notes: Poem by Hannah Flagg Gould. The 'Pee, dee, dee' bird is the chickadee.

lessons.title: Lesson XLIV: The Nettle
steps: New words: botany (study of plants), magnifying glass, enchantment, asunder (apart), remedy, conveyed (carried)
Read it as a dialogue: your child is Anna, you are Papa
Narrate: what did Anna discover when she looked at the nettle closely?
If you can, look at a leaf or flower with a magnifying glass
questions: What did Papa use to soothe the sting?
What makes the nettle sting?
What did the 'little cloud' from the flower do?
answers: Juice from a dock leaf
Hollow bristles with tiny bags of juice at their base
Carried pollen to the seeds of another nettle so they could grow
lessons.notes: The medical use of nettle stings 'instead of blisters' is outdated medicine.

lessons.title: Lesson XLV: The Tempest
steps: New words: deep (the ocean), blast, breakers
Read the poem aloud, quietly at first and then with mounting fear
Memorize: the fifth stanza (“But his little daughter whispered…”)
questions: What did the captain shout?
What did his little daughter ask him?
How did the night end?
answers: “We are lost!”
Isn't God upon the ocean, just the same as on the land?
They anchored safely in harbor in the morning
lessons.notes: Poem by James T. Fields.

lessons.title: Lesson XLVI: The Creator
steps: New words: blown (in full bloom), odor, lair, dazzling, perfection, lore, encompassed
Read the prose and Keble's verses aloud slowly
Narrate: what three things are shown, and who is greater than each?
questions: What is shown as beautiful, strong, and glorious?
What is the 'book' that anyone may read, in Keble's poem?
answers: The rose, the lion, and the sun
The works of God in nature
lessons.notes: Adapted from Anna Laetitia Barbauld's Hymns in Prose; the verses are by John Keble. A devotional reading.

lessons.title: Lesson XLVII: The Horse
steps: New words: immense, cavalry, impetuosity (fury), dexterously (skillfully), symmetry, toman (a Persian coin), deliverance, gallant
Read it as a conversation: your child reads Frank, you read Uncle Thomas
Narrate: tell one of Uncle Thomas's three horse stories
questions: How do hunters in South America catch wild horses?
Why wouldn't the Arab sell his mare?
How many sailors did the planter and his horse save?
answers: With a lasso thrown from horseback
He loved her too much to sell her for any price
Fourteen
lessons.notes: Adapted from Bingley. The planter blows brandy into his horse's nostrils, an old practice not to copy; prices are in 1870s dollars.

lessons.title: Lesson XLVIII: Emulation
steps: New words: emulation (rivalry), competition, excelled (surpassed), rivals, anecdote, tuition
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Narrate: what did the farmer's son do when his rival stopped coming to school?
questions: Who were the two rivals for the head of the class?
Why did the widow's son leave school?
How did the farmer's son help him?
answers: A rich farmer's son and a poor widow's son
His mother could no longer pay for tuition and books, so he had to work
He paid for his rival's books and tuition from his own pocket money
lessons.notes: Schools then charged tuition; good place to talk about competing without envy.

lessons.title: Lesson XLIX: The Sandpiper
steps: New words: sandpiper, driftwood, bleached, scud, close-reefed, stanch (firm), wroth (angry)
Read the poem aloud; let your child say “One little sandpiper and I” each time
Memorize: the last stanza (“Comrade, where wilt thou be to-night…”)
Look up a picture of a sandpiper
questions: What is the poet gathering on the beach?
Why does she not fear for the sandpiper in the storm?
answers: Driftwood
They are both God's children
lessons.notes: Poem by Celia Thaxter, written on the Isles of Shoals.

lessons.title: Lesson L: The Right Way
steps: New words: particular, dominie (Scottish schoolmaster), reflecting, overcast, impracticable (not possible), anxiety, devise
Read the story aloud, you as Jenny and your child as Andrew
Narrate: what simple, honest answer did Andrew finally find?
questions: Why couldn't Jenny get home?
Why wouldn't Andrew make up an excuse for being late?
What did Andrew finally do?
answers: Old Donald had pulled the footbridge to the other side of the creek
He would not tell a lie
Asked the schoolmaster for permission to take her home
lessons.notes: Adapted from a story by Frank R. Stockton.

lessons.title: Lesson LI: The Golden Rule
steps: New words: integrity (honesty), conviction, temptation, assails (attacks), conflict, gruff
Read the story aloud together
Narrate: tell Susan's struggle on the way home and what she decided
questions: What is the Golden Rule?
What mistake did Farmer Thompson make?
Why did Susan refuse the shilling?
answers: Do to others what you would want them to do to you
He gave Susan two bills instead of one
She did not want to be paid for doing right
lessons.notes: The mother points to the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10); you may want to read it too.

lessons.title: Lesson LII: The Snow Man
steps: New words: pipe (whistle), shrink, triumph, realm
Read the poem aloud
Copywork: “Than be a man who walks with men, / But has a frozen heart!”
Narrate: what would the poet rather be than a cold-hearted man?
questions: Who built the snow man?
What does 'a frozen heart' mean?
answers: A schoolboy
Being unkind and uncaring toward others
lessons.notes: Poem by Marian Douglas.

lessons.title: Lesson LIII: Robinson Crusoe's House
steps: New words: habitation, pale (fence of stakes), fortification, egress (way out)
Read the selection aloud together
Narrate: describe how Crusoe built and improved his home
Draw a plan of Crusoe's tent, wall, and cave
questions: What did Crusoe build around his tent?
Why did he dig farther into the rock?
What did he make for himself once the cave was bigger?
answers: A wall of turf against a fence of posts and cables
His goods were in a heap with no room to turn around
A table and a chair
lessons.notes: Adapted from Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe (1719). Pair it with the next lesson.

lessons.title: Lesson LIV: Robinson Crusoe's Dress
steps: New words: buskins (leg coverings), spatterdashes (gaiters), barbarous (clumsy), thongs, frog (a loop), pouches, monstrous
Read the selection aloud in Crusoe's voice
Narrate: describe Crusoe from his cap down to his feet
Draw Crusoe in his goatskin clothes
questions: What were almost all of Crusoe's clothes made of?
What hung from his belt in place of a sword and dagger?
Next to his gun, what was his most necessary item?
answers: Goatskin
A little saw and a hatchet
His goatskin umbrella
lessons.notes: From Defoe's Robinson Crusoe. The book's notes explain that the story was based on Alexander Selkirk's years alone on an island off Chile. 'Mahometan whiskers' is an old phrase for a Turkish-style mustache.

lessons.title: Lesson LV: Somebody's Darling
steps: New words: bayonet, lingering, matted, enshrined (cherished), wafted, yearning
Read the poem aloud quietly and slowly
Narrate: who is 'somebody,' and why does the poet keep repeating the word?
questions: Where does the poem take place?
What is carved on the soldier's grave marker?
answers: In a hospital ward for wounded soldiers
“Somebody's darling slumbers here.”
lessons.notes: A Civil War poem by Marie Ravenel de la Coste (not named in the book) about a young soldier who dies of his wounds. Preview it for a sensitive child.

lessons.title: Lesson LVI: Knowledge Is Power
steps: New words: bustling, meekly, restraint, trenches, fertile, produce
Read it as a dialogue: your child is the little man saying “I see!”
Narrate: give the old man's three examples of power used well and badly
questions: What did the bustling little man think was always excellent?
What does the old man say knowledge really is?
What three examples did the old man give?
answers: Knowledge
An increase of power, which can be good or bad
A horse, a pond of water, and a ship's sail

lessons.title: Lesson LVII: Good Will
steps: New words: character, purpose, principles, capacity (ability), sordid (mean, greedy)
Read the talk aloud, taking turns by paragraph
Narrate: compare Thomas and James at their work
questions: Why did Thomas do nothing well?
What did James have that was better than talent?
What one word of advice does the writer leave the boys?
answers: For lack of good will, not lack of talent
Good will in his work
Good will
lessons.notes: Adapted from J. T. Trowbridge.

lessons.title: Lesson LVIII: A Chinese Story
steps: New words: near-sighted, tablet, inscription, optics (eyes), palm (prize), mandarin (Chinese official)
Read the poem aloud; you are Chang, your child is Ching
Narrate: how did the priest settle the quarrel?
questions: What were Chang and Ching arguing about?
Why did each one secretly visit the temple first?
Why could neither of them have read the tablet?
answers: Which of them could see better
To read the tablet up close so they could pretend to read it from far away
It had been moved inside the temple the day before
lessons.notes: Poem by Christopher Pearse Cranch. The made-up 'Chinese' names are a 19th-century joke; talk about how the humor is in the two cheaters, not in where they are from.

lessons.title: Lesson LIX: The Way to Be Happy
steps: New words: cultivating, unpopular, sacrifices, promote, generosity, infallible (certain), intercourse (dealings with others)
Read the lesson aloud, taking turns by paragraph
Narrate: tell the two examples the writer gives of giving up your place
Plan one kind thing to do for a brother, sister, or friend today
questions: What is the only way to make friends, according to the lesson?
What did the boy offer James at the school stove?
What did he offer Henry at the ball game?
answers: By being friendly to others
His warm place by the fire
His place in the game while he rested
lessons.notes: The heading misprints this lesson as 'LXX'; it is Lesson LIX. The lesson claims anyone not loved is always at fault; you may want to soften that for a child who is struggling with friendships.

lessons.title: Lesson LX: The Giraffe, or Camelopard
steps: New words: brilliant, diversified (varied), naturalist, specimen, baffled, conjectured (guessed), carbine (short gun)
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Narrate: describe a giraffe from head to hoof
Look at a photo of a giraffe and compare it with the description
questions: On what continent do giraffes live?
How tall is a full-grown giraffe, according to the lesson?
How does a giraffe defend itself?
answers: Africa
Seventeen or eighteen feet
By kicking with its hind legs
lessons.notes: Le Vaillant was an 18th-century French explorer who shot the giraffe as a specimen, as naturalists did then. Giraffes are now protected in many places.

lessons.title: Lesson LXI: The Lost Child
steps: New words: distracted, suspense, traversed, sympathized, declivity (downward slope), procession
Read the story aloud together
Narrate: tell how the whole village searched for the child
questions: How did the child get lost?
What signal would tell everyone the child was found?
Which Bible parable does the ending recall?
answers: He was separated from his brothers and sisters while picking berries
A gun fired
The lost sheep (joy over one that was found)
lessons.notes: Ends with a reflection on the parable of the lost sheep (Luke 15).

lessons.title: Lesson LXII: Which?
steps: New words: aye (always), surveyed, crown (an English coin), wayward, turbulent, courteous
Read the poem aloud slowly; pause at each child's bed
Narrate: why couldn't the parents give away any of their seven children?
questions: What did Robert offer the poor family?
How many children did they have?
What did the parents decide?
answers: A house and land for life, if they gave him one child
Seven
To keep all seven and trust God for the rest
lessons.notes: Poem by Mrs. Ethel Lynn Beers. Giving a child to a wealthy relative was not unheard of then; reassure a younger child as needed.

lessons.title: Lesson LXIII: The Pet Fawn
steps: New words: fawn, caressed, dilated, spectators, intercept, betrayed (showed), cowed
Read the story aloud
Narrate: tell the chase from the store steps to the forest
questions: What made the tame fawn suddenly run?
Where did the fawn swim to escape?
How did the lady learn what happened to her fawn?
answers: A hunter's hound came near
Across a bay of the lake to the forest
A hunter brought her its collar; he had shot it
lessons.notes: By Susan Fenimore Cooper. It has a sad ending; preview for tender-hearted children. A good talk about why wild animals don't make safe pets.

lessons.title: Lesson LXIV: Annie's Dream
steps: New words: natural philosophy (old name for physical science), evaporation, degree, sprites
Read the story aloud; you and your child take turns as Annie and the sprites
Narrate: tell how the water sprites changed into frost and back
Set out a dish of water and watch it slowly evaporate over a few days
questions: Was Annie right that water must reach 212 degrees to evaporate?
What did the water sprites turn into on the cold window?
What happened when Annie breathed on the frost?
answers: No; 212 degrees is boiling, but water evaporates at lower temperatures
Frost sprites (frost)
It melted into a drop of water
lessons.notes: A gentle science lesson on evaporation and frost dressed as a dream.

lessons.title: Lesson LXV: My Ghost
steps: Read the poem aloud, building suspense toward the last line
Narrate: retell the walk past the old house and graveyard, and what the 'ghost' turned out to be
Go outside on a sunny or moonlit day and watch your own shadow copy you
questions: Why didn't Katie go on the walk?
What did the 'ghost' do as the speaker walked?
What was the ghost really?
answers: She had been naughty and cried to go
It copied everything she did
Her own shadow
lessons.notes: Poem by Sarah M. B. Piatt. Spooky but with a gentle twist.

lessons.title: Lesson LXVI: The Elephant
steps: New words: quadruped, pendulous (hanging down), proboscis (trunk), stratagem, docile (teachable), asylum (refuge), nabob (an Indian prince)
Your child reads the lesson aloud
Narrate: tell one of the three elephant stories
questions: How can you tell an Asian elephant from an African one, according to the lesson?
How did the London elephant get the sixpence?
What did the nabob's elephant do on the crowded road?
answers: The Asian has five toes, the African three
He blew air against the wall so the coin slid toward him
Carefully lifted or stepped around the sick people so no one was hurt
lessons.notes: Old natural history: elephants are not shaped like hogs, and the toe count is not a reliable difference. The ivory trade the lesson mentions is now banned to protect elephants. One story includes a drunken soldier.

lessons.title: Lesson LXVII: Dare to Do Right (Part 1)
steps: New words: waistcoat (vest), overwhelmed, novelty, ablution (washing), sneered, bully
Read the selection aloud together
Narrate: what happened on Arthur's first night at Rugby?
questions: What did Arthur do that made the room fall silent?
What did the bully throw at him?
How did Tom defend Arthur?
answers: Knelt by his bed to pray
A slipper
He threw his boot at the bully and dared anyone to want the other one
lessons.notes: Adapted from Tom Brown's School Days by Thomas Hughes. Rugby was an English boarding school; the 'sixth-form boy' was an older student who kept order.

lessons.title: Lesson LXVIII: Dare to Do Right (Part 2)
steps: New words: leaven (to change gradually), loathed (hated), braggart, testimony, faltered, subtle
Read the conclusion aloud
Narrate: what did Tom resolve during the night, and what happened in the morning?
questions: Why did Tom feel like a coward?
What prayer did Tom say the next morning?
What happened after Tom knelt to pray?
answers: He had stopped kneeling to pray because he feared the others' laughter, though little Arthur dared to
“God be merciful to me a sinner!”
Two boys followed at once, and soon nearly all the others did too
lessons.notes: Mentions Dr. Thomas Arnold, the famous headmaster, and the story of Elijah hearing the 'still, small voice' (1 Kings 19).

lessons.title: Lesson LXIX: The Wreck of the Hesperus
steps: New words: skipper, veering, flaw (gust), brine, amain (with force), spar, helm, shrouds (mast ropes)
Read the ballad aloud with drama; your child reads the daughter's questions
Narrate: what warning did the skipper ignore, and what happened?
Memorize: the first stanza (“It was the schooner Hesperus…”)
questions: What warning did the old sailor give?
Why did the skipper tie his daughter to the mast?
Where was the ship wrecked?
answers: The ring around the moon meant a hurricane was coming, so they should put into port
To keep her from being washed overboard in the storm
On the reef of Norman's Woe near Gloucester, Massachusetts
lessons.notes: Poem by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. The father and daughter both die; preview for sensitive children.

lessons.title: Lesson LXX: Anecdotes of Birds
steps: New words: copse (thicket), sagacious (wise), impertinent (rude), vehemence (force), migration, domicile (home), recognition
Read the three bird stories aloud, one at a time
Narrate: choose one story (Yarico the hen, the clever parrot, or the house martins) and tell it
questions: How did Yarico protect her chicks from the fox cub?
What trick did the parrot play on the dogs?
How do we know the young martins came back the next spring?
answers: She hid them in the hedge behind her and stood in front to hold the fox off
She dropped bread to call them, then screamed “Get out, dogs!”
Four martins flew straight into the same room and twittered joyfully
lessons.notes: By 'Hall' (as named in the book's contents). In one story boys shoot at a sparrow with blowguns.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXI: The Rainbow Pilgrimage
steps: New words: recovering, wintergreen, imposed upon (fooled), drabbling (muddying), porcupine, pilgrimage, quizzing (teasing)
Read the story aloud together
Narrate: tell Gracie's chase after the end of the rainbow and how she was found
questions: What did Rufus say was at the end of the rainbow?
Why didn't Gracie answer when searchers called her name?
How did she know it was really her brother on the log?
answers: Purses of money and pots of gold and silver
She feared they were Indians tricking her
He called her secret family pet name
lessons.notes: By Grace Greenwood (Sara J. Lippincott). Gracie's fear of 'Indians' reflects frontier prejudice of the time; worth a short talk.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXII: The Old Oaken Bucket
steps: New words: cataract (waterfall), exquisite, poised (balanced), goblet, nectar, reverts (returns)
Read the poem aloud; let your child join in the refrain
Memorize: the refrain (“The old oaken bucket, the ironbound bucket…”)
Narrate: what scenes of his childhood does the poet remember?
questions: What does the poet remember drinking from?
When did he most enjoy the water?
What would he not trade it for?
answers: The old oaken bucket in the well
At noon, coming back hot from the field
Not even a goblet of the gods' nectar
lessons.notes: Poem by Samuel Woodworth; it was later a popular song.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXIII: The Sermon on the Mount
steps: New words: disciple, inherit, revile, persecute, publicans (tax collectors), mote (speck), hypocrite
Read the passage aloud slowly
Memorize: one Beatitude your child chooses
Narrate: tell the parable of the two builders at the end
questions: Name two groups Jesus calls blessed.
How does Jesus say to treat our enemies?
Where did the wise man build his house?
answers: Any two: the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, etc.
Love them, bless them, do good to them, and pray for them
On a rock
lessons.notes: Selections from Matthew 5–7 (King James Version).

lessons.title: Lesson LXXIV: The Young Witness
steps: New words: witness, counsel (lawyer), confidingly, profane, perjury (lying under oath), chaff
Read the courtroom scene aloud, you as the judge and your child as Emily
Narrate: how did Emily show the judge she understood an oath?
questions: Why did the prisoner's lawyer want Emily rejected?
Which commandment did Emily point to?
What had her mother done the night before?
answers: He said she did not understand the nature of an oath
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbor (the Ninth)
Heard her say the commandments and prayed with her to tell the truth
lessons.notes: By S. H. Hammond.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXV: King Solomon and the Ants
steps: New words: interpreted (explained), greet, welfare, train (followers), flatteries
Read the poem aloud; your child reads the ants' words and the queen's
Memorize: “The wise and strong should seek / The welfare of the weak;”
Narrate: what did Solomon do, and what did the Queen of Sheba learn from it?
questions: What special gift did King Solomon have in the poem?
What did the ants fear?
What did the queen say makes a state happy?
answers: He understood the languages of all creatures
That the king's party would crush them
A ruler who listens more to the poor than to the flattery of the great
lessons.notes: Poem by John Greenleaf Whittier, based on an old legend (the Queen of Sheba's visit is in 1 Kings 10).

lessons.title: Lesson LXXVI: Rivermouth Theater
steps: New words: conclave (private meeting), managerial, deducting, career, audience, injunction (command), maelstrom (whirlpool)
Read it aloud, enjoying the narrator's joking tone
Narrate: tell what went wrong at the tenth performance
questions: What was the price of admission?
Why did the narrator play all the main parts?
What ended the theater for good?
answers: Twenty pins
Because he owned the theater
His arrow hit Pepper Whitcomb in the mouth, and Grandfather Nutter forbade more plays
lessons.notes: From The Story of a Bad Boy by Thomas Bailey Aldrich. Remind children not to try the William Tell scene with real bows.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXVII: Alfred the Great
steps: New words: monastery, invasion, disguised, university, translated, enlightened
Read the lesson aloud, taking turns by paragraph
Narrate: tell the story of the burnt cakes or of Alfred in the Danish camp
Find England and Denmark on a map
questions: How did Alfred win his mother's book of poems?
How did Alfred spy on the Danish army?
How did Alfred mark the hours of his day?
answers: He was the first of the four sons to learn to read it
He disguised himself as a harper and entered their camp
By burning candles of equal length
lessons.notes: Alfred ruled Wessex in the 800s; the burnt-cakes tale is a well-loved legend.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXVIII: Living on a Farm
steps: Read the poem aloud with a happy, remembering voice
Copywork: “When I was living on a farm.”
Narrate: what does the poet remember about each season on the farm?
questions: What were the neighbors talking about at church?
What autumn gathering does the poet remember?
answers: The crops and the weather (needing rain or sun)
The husking bee
lessons.notes: The heading misprints this lesson as 'LXXVII'; it is Lesson LXXVIII. A husking bee was a party for stripping husks from corn.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXIX: Hugh Idle and Mr. Toil (Part 1)
steps: New words: agreeable, affirmed, sedate (calm), sociably, resemblance, visage (face), quoth (said)
Read the story aloud together
Narrate: where did Hugh think he saw Mr. Toil on the road?
questions: Why did Hugh run away from school?
Who was the 'Mr. Toil' among the haymakers?
Who did Hugh see overseeing the carpenters?
answers: He disliked the strict schoolmaster, Mr. Toil
Mr. Toil's brother, a farmer
Another brother of Mr. Toil, a carpenter
lessons.notes: Adapted from Nathaniel Hawthorne's 'Little Daffydowndilly.' Mr. Toil carries a cane, as old-time teachers did.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXX: Hugh Idle and Mr. Toil (Part 2)
steps: New words: venture, dismay, enlist, composedly (calmly), innumerable, approbation (approval)
Read the conclusion aloud
Narrate: who was the stranger, and what did Hugh learn?
questions: What did the fiddler call himself?
Where did Hugh's long walk end?
Who was the stranger walking with Hugh?
answers: Master Pleasure
Back at the schoolhouse; they had walked in a circle
Mr. Toil himself
lessons.notes: Talk about the idea that every kind of life, even play, takes work.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXI: Burning the Fallow
steps: New words: abating (lessening), listlessly, fallow (a new clearing full of brush), canopy, appalling, lurid (dull red), igniting
Read the selection aloud, slowing down as the fire closes in
Narrate: how was the family trapped, and what saved them?
questions: Who started the fire?
Why couldn't they escape to the lake?
What put the fire out?
answers: John Thomas, the hired boy
The burning swamp lay between the house and the lake
A sudden thunderstorm with heavy rain
lessons.notes: Adapted from Roughing It in the Bush by Susanna Moodie, about pioneer life in the Canadian backwoods. A good time to talk about fire safety.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXII: The Dying Soldiers
steps: New words: sodden (soaked), phantasy, blent (mingled), tidings (news), anguish, repressed
Read the poem aloud quietly
Narrate: what did the two enemy soldiers say to each other before they died?
questions: Where were the two soldiers' homes?
Who was waiting for each of them?
What did they do before they died?
answers: New Hampshire and Georgia
A wife and a golden-haired girl; a dark-eyed little girl
Forgave each other and clasped hands
lessons.notes: A Civil War poem about a Union and a Confederate soldier dying side by side. Sad and serious; preview for younger children.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXIII: The Attack on Nymwegen
steps: New words: morion (helmet), freebooter (plunderer), musketeer, burghers (townspeople), garrison, flotilla, quay (wharf), truculent (fierce)
Read the selection aloud together
Narrate: why did Martin Schenk's night attack fail?
Find the Netherlands and the Waal River on a map
questions: What was happening in the house Schenk broke into?
Why didn't most of Schenk's boats arrive?
How did Schenk die?
answers: A wedding feast
The flooded river swept them past the landing place
His overloaded boat sank and his heavy armor dragged him to the bottom of the Waal
lessons.notes: From John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands; the attack took place in 1589 during the Dutch wars. Contains battle violence.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXIV: The Seasons
steps: Read all four short poems aloud, one per season
Choose your favorite and copy two lines of it
Narrate: what signs of each season does each poem mention?
questions: Which season does the 'high tide of the year' describe?
In 'Autumn,' what has the old autumn gathered up?
What does the 'Winter' poet still love about winter?
answers: Summer
Gold (golden leaves and harvest)
Its chilly greeting, snowstorms, and long nights
lessons.notes: Spring by H. G. Adams; Summer by James Russell Lowell; Autumn by Thomas Hood; Winter by Ludwig Hölty, translated by C. T. Brooks.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXV: Brandywine Ford (Part 1)
steps: New words: interminable (endless), turbid (muddy), discerned (made out), seething, inundation (flood), immerged
Read the selection aloud, building the suspense
Narrate: what happened to Gilbert and Roger at the ford?
questions: What was Roger?
What roaring sound did Gilbert hear?
How did Gilbert save himself from the flood?
answers: Gilbert's horse
A dam bursting upstream
He grabbed a log caught on the timbers and climbed onto it
lessons.notes: Adapted from Bayard Taylor's novel The Story of Kennett, set in Pennsylvania.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXVI: Brandywine Ford (Part 2)
steps: New words: prospect (hope), breasted (faced bravely), numb, relaxed, emotion
Read the conclusion aloud; your child reads the farmer's story of Roger
Narrate: how did Roger bring help to Gilbert?
questions: How did the rescuer get Gilbert off the log without a rope?
How did the farmer know something was wrong?
What did Gilbert do before going into the farmhouse?
answers: He threw Gilbert the end of Roger's bridle and pulled him onto the saddle
A saddled horse kept neighing, stamping, and leading him toward the creek
He hugged and kissed Roger's head

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXVII: The Best Capital
steps: New words: eulogy (speech of praise), cherished, appreciated, conscientious, legacy, capital (money used to start a business)
Read the selection aloud together
Narrate: what did Uncle Fritz say made John Brooke a great man?
questions: Why did John Brooke leave one of his jobs?
What had John done for his family before he died?
What does Uncle Fritz call 'the best capital'?
answers: His employer wanted him to help cheat
Paid every debt and saved enough to keep them comfortable
Simple, genuine goodness
lessons.notes: Adapted from Louisa May Alcott's Little Men; John Brooke is Meg's husband from Little Women. It opens at his funeral.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXVIII: The Inchcape Rock
steps: New words: keel, buoy, surge, joyance, scoured (roamed over), methinks, knell
Read the ballad aloud with feeling; your child reads Sir Ralph's lines
Memorize: the third and fourth stanzas (the Abbot's bell)
Narrate: how did Sir Ralph's wicked trick come back on him?
questions: Who put the bell on the Inchcape Rock, and why?
What did Sir Ralph the Rover do to the bell?
What happened to Sir Ralph's ship?
answers: The Abbot of Aberbrothok, to warn sailors of the hidden rock
Cut it loose so it sank
It struck the Inchcape Rock in the dark and sank
lessons.notes: Poem by Robert Southey, based on an old Scottish legend. The Bell Rock Lighthouse now stands on the real reef.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXIX: My Mother's Grave
steps: New words: effaced (wiped out), pettishly (crossly), domestic (servant), reproach, ingratitude, manifold
Read the selection aloud slowly
Narrate: what small unkindness did the writer regret all her life?
questions: What did the sick mother ask her daughter to bring?
Why couldn't the girl apologize that night?
What did she find in the morning?
answers: A glass of water
